title: Something has happened
lede: If something has already gone wrong, this page is the fastest route to the right help. Take a breath first. You have more time than it feels like, and the things that matter most take about five minutes.

steps.title: Stay calm, and tell them they are not in trouble
steps.body: Your reaction in the first minute decides how much they tell you in the next hour. An Garda Síochána puts this first in its guidance to parents: stay calm, reassure your child, let them know they are not in trouble and that you are there to help. Whatever they did, what has been done to them is the crime.

steps.title: Do not delete anything
steps.body: Block the person, but leave the messages, the images and the account where they are. Deleting destroys the evidence that lets police identify them. The UK's National Crime Agency is specific about this: deactivate an account rather than deleting it, because deactivated data can still be retrieved.
steps.source: NCMEC, National Crime Agency, An Garda Síochána

steps.title: Screenshot before you block
steps.body: Capture the conversation, the profile and anything they sent. Then block. Doing it in that order takes an extra two minutes and is the difference between a report that goes somewhere and one that doesn't.

evidence.title: What to save before you block
evidence.intro: Official guidance names the first four. The last two are SafeStart's own practical advice rather than an official instruction, and they make a report much easier to act on.
official: The messages themselves, including anything already deleted from view
Any images or videos that were sent or received
Phone numbers, and bank or payment details if money was asked for
The web addresses of any page where images have been shared
practical: The exact username, display name and profile link, which change often
Dates and times, or a screenshot that shows them
evidence.note: Save screenshots somewhere outside the app itself, so that a deleted account doesn't take them with it. Your own photo library or an email to yourself is fine.

situations.label: Someone is threatening to share nude images
situations.summary: Sometimes called sextortion. Someone has an intimate image of your child, or claims to, and is demanding money or more images.

keyAdvice.title: Do not pay
keyAdvice.body: Every official body agrees on this. NCMEC: cooperating or paying rarely stops the blackmail. The FBI: offenders often release the material whether or not they are paid. Cybertip.ca: never pay money and never send additional nudes.

keyAdvice.title: If you have already paid, stop there
keyAdvice.body: The National Crime Agency's line is the one worth holding on to: if you have paid, don't panic, but don't pay anything more. Paying once does not make things worse. Paying again does.

keyAdvice.title: Block, but keep everything
keyAdvice.body: NCMEC is explicit: block the suspect, but do not delete your profile or messages, because they can help stop the blackmailer.

keyAdvice.title: Tell your child this is not their fault
keyAdvice.body: NCMEC's own words are worth repeating to them directly: the blackmailer is to blame, not you. Even if you made a choice you regret, what they are doing is a crime. The FBI's advice to parents is to make clear that your first move will be to help, always.

situations.context: Financial sextortion disproportionately targets teenage boys. The National Crime Agency identifies males aged 14 to 17 as particularly at risk, and the Canadian Centre for Child Protection reports that 83% of sextortion victims were male where gender was known. That said, the FBI has interviewed victims as young as 8, of both genders, and notes the only common trait among victims is internet access. If you have a daughter, this still applies to her.

situations.label: An adult has been contacting my child
situations.summary: Someone older has been messaging your child, and it has moved somewhere private, or turned sexual, or they have asked to meet.

keyAdvice.title: Report it to the national body, not just the platform
keyAdvice.body: Platform reports get the account removed. A report to your country's child protection body is what gets it investigated. Do both, and do the national one first.

keyAdvice.title: Keep the account open for now
keyAdvice.body: Your instinct will be to delete the app. Preserve it until you have reported, then decide. A deleted account takes the evidence with it.

keyAdvice.title: Ask gently, and ask once
keyAdvice.body: You need to know roughly what happened and how long it has been going on. You do not need every detail, and pressing for detail is the part that makes children stop talking. The professionals who take your report are trained for that conversation.

situations.context: A common pattern is that contact starts inside a game or a public server and quickly moves to a private app such as Discord, Snapchat or WhatsApp. If your child has been asked to move a conversation somewhere more private, that on its own is worth reporting.

situations.label: An image of my child is being shared
situations.summary: A nude or sexual image of your child, taken when they were under 18, is circulating or has been posted.

keyAdvice.title: Use Take It Down, and understand why StopNCII will turn you away
keyAdvice.body: Take It Down is NCMEC's free service for images taken of someone under 18. It works anywhere, not just the US. StopNCII is the adult equivalent and requires the person to have been 18 or over both when the image was taken and now, so it will reject a case involving a child. Parents land on the wrong one all the time.

keyAdvice.title: The image does not leave your device
keyAdvice.body: Take It Down generates a digital fingerprint, a hash, on your own device. The image itself is never uploaded. Participating platforms match the hash and remove the content. This is worth explaining to a teenager who is terrified of handing the image to anyone.

keyAdvice.title: In the UK, Report Remove is designed for this
keyAdvice.body: Report Remove is run jointly by Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation for under-18s in the UK. The young person reports it themselves, verifies their age, and gets updates plus counsellor support through their Childline account.

situations.context: There is no separate Canadian hash-removal service. Canadian families use Take It Down, and NeedHelpNow.ca has step-by-step removal instructions for each major platform.

situations.label: My child is being bullied or harassed
situations.summary: Sustained cruelty, exclusion, threats or humiliation from people your child may well know.

keyAdvice.title: Screenshot the pattern, not just the worst message
keyAdvice.body: A single message rarely gets acted on. A run of them over days does. Capture dates where you can.

keyAdvice.title: Report inside the platform first
keyAdvice.body: For bullying, the platform is genuinely the right first stop, and most have a specific bullying or harassment category that routes faster than a general report.

keyAdvice.title: Involve the school if the people involved are from school
keyAdvice.body: Most online bullying between classmates is a school matter with an online surface. Schools in all four countries have a duty here and are usually better placed to stop it than any platform.

situations.context: The UK's CEOP Safety Centre does not handle bullying and will redirect you to Childline. That is not a brush-off, it is a routing decision, and Childline is the better service for it.

situations.label: They have seen something disturbing
situations.summary: Violent, sexual or otherwise upsetting content that has stayed with them.

keyAdvice.title: Deal with the child before the settings
keyAdvice.body: The instinct is to go and fix the controls. Do that later today. Right now the useful thing is letting them describe it, telling them it was not their fault for seeing it, and not reacting with alarm that they then have to manage.

keyAdvice.title: Report the content where they saw it
keyAdvice.body: If it was child sexual abuse material, report it to your national body rather than the platform, and do not download, forward or screenshot it. That is the one situation where screenshotting is the wrong move and can itself be an offence.

keyAdvice.title: Then tighten the setting that let it through
keyAdvice.body: Once they are settled, the relevant SafeStart guide will have the specific control. Usually it is a content maturity or restricted mode setting, or an autoplay behaviour.

situations.context: Do not go looking for the content to see how bad it was. If it is illegal material, viewing and saving it creates problems for you and for any investigation.

police.line: That is NCMEC's own guidance too. Their CyberTipline is for reporting, not for emergencies.
police.nonEmergency: For a non-emergency report, contact your local FBI field office, call 1-800-CALL-FBI, or use tips.fbi.gov.

bodies.name: NCMEC CyberTipline
bodies.what: The national reporting route for online child exploitation, grooming, and child sexual abuse material. Reports go to law enforcement.

bodies.name: Take It Down
bodies.what: Free removal service for intimate images taken of someone under 18. The image stays on your device.

bodies.name: NCMEC — get help now
bodies.what: Support hub, including help for families after a report.

bodies.name: FBI IC3
bodies.what: Intake for cyber-enabled crime. Useful for the record, but note their own wording: you will not be contacted by IC3. Do not rely on it for help in a live situation.

police.line: That is the National Crime Agency's guidance for anyone at immediate risk of harm.
police.nonEmergency: Call 101 for a non-emergency report to your local police.

bodies.name: CEOP Safety Centre
bodies.what: Reports go to a Child Protection Advisor at CEOP, which is a command of the National Crime Agency. For online sexual abuse or concerning contact. Not for bullying.

bodies.name: Report Remove
bodies.what: For under-18s in the UK to get a nude image of themselves removed. Run by Childline with the Internet Watch Foundation.

bodies.name: Internet Watch Foundation
bodies.what: Anonymous reporting of child sexual abuse imagery, including AI-generated and drawn material, for removal.

bodies.name: NSPCC Helpline
bodies.what: For adults worried about a child. Free, and you do not have to give your name.
bodies.phone: 0808 800 5000 — phone 10am to 4pm Mon to Fri, email help@nspcc.org.uk 11am to 4pm daily
bodies.caveatNote: Not a 24-hour service. Childline, for your child, is 24 hours on 0800 1111.

police.line: That is Cybertip.ca's own guidance. They forward their reports to police as well.
police.nonEmergency: Contact your local police service. Cybertip forwards its reports to police as well.

bodies.name: Cybertip.ca
bodies.what: Canada's national tipline, operated by the Canadian Centre for Child Protection. Covers child sexual abuse material, grooming, luring, intimate images, sextortion and AI deepfakes.
bodies.phone: Staffed 8:30am to 4:00pm Central, Mon to Fri. Online reporting is open at all times.

bodies.name: NeedHelpNow.ca
bodies.what: For under-18s whose images are being shared. Has the clearest step-by-step removal instructions for Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Discord and others that we found anywhere.

bodies.name: Take It Down
bodies.what: There is no Canadian hash-removal service, so Canadian families use NCMEC's, which works internationally.

police.line: An Garda Síochána are clear that urgent situations should always be reported to them directly, and that a hotline report does not replace it.
police.nonEmergency: Your local Garda station. Garda Confidential is 1800 666 111, and the Garda child sexual abuse reporting line is 1800 555 222.

bodies.name: An Garda Síochána
bodies.what: Report directly. Hotline.ie says plainly that reporting to them is not a substitute for notifying the Gardaí.
bodies.phone: 999 or 112 in an emergency, 1800 555 222 for child sexual abuse reporting

bodies.name: Hotline.ie
bodies.what: Reporting for child sexual abuse material, grooming, intimate image abuse and sexual extortion. Anonymous except for intimate image abuse reports.

bodies.name: ISPCC Childline
bodies.what: 24-hour listening service for children and young people up to 18. For your child rather than for you.

bodies.name: Coimisiún na Meán
bodies.what: The regulator. Use this when a platform has failed to act, not as a first step. You need to have reported to the platform first, and they will not accept child sexual abuse material.

platforms.name: Roblox
platforms.route: In app: the shield or Report icon in the menu, or the three dots on a profile, chat or item. As a parent you can also report from Parental Controls → Settings → Communications using your child's account.

platforms.name: Fortnite and Epic Games
platforms.route: In game, or the web form below. Epic has the clearest reporting route of any platform here.

platforms.name: Discord
platforms.route: Discord has a dedicated form for parents and guardians, which does not require you to be in the server. If you have access to your teen's account you can also report from inside the app.
platforms.urlLabel: How to contact Discord Safety for parents

platforms.name: Snapchat
platforms.route: Press and hold on the content to report in app. Snapchat also has web forms, including one specifically for leaked nudity and sexual content.

platforms.name: Instagram
platforms.route: Reporting is in app. The help pages describe the process rather than offering a separate form, so a parent generally needs access to the account to report content.

platforms.name: TikTok
platforms.route: Press and hold on the video, comment or message, then Report. We could not verify a working web reporting form, so in-app is the reliable route.

platforms.name: YouTube
platforms.route: Reporting requires you to be signed in to a Google account. There is no signed-out web reporting tool, so you will need to be on an account to report a video, channel or comment.

platforms.name: Minecraft
platforms.route: Use the in-game player reporting tool. We could not verify a web reporting form. For Microsoft accounts, the Xbox complaint route below also applies.

platforms.name: Xbox and Microsoft
platforms.route: File a complaint about a player through Xbox support.

platformsNote: Platform reporting routes move often, and several of these companies have deliberately pushed reporting inside the app and behind a login. Where we could not confirm a working web form we have said so rather than guessing. If a link here fails, the in-app route described alongside it still works.

lines.text: You are not in trouble. I am glad you told me.
lines.note: An Garda Síochána put reassurance ahead of every practical step in their guidance to parents, and it is the thing most parents skip.

lines.text: This is not your fault, even if you made a choice you regret. What they are doing is a crime.
lines.note: Close to NCMEC's own wording, which is worth using almost verbatim.

lines.text: My first move is to help. Always.
lines.note: The FBI's suggested framing for parents.

lines.text: We are going to sort this out together, and I am not going to take your phone away as a punishment for telling me.
lines.note: SafeStart's own addition. Fear of losing the device is one of the most common reasons children don't tell anyone.

standingLine: Reporting to a hotline does not replace reporting to the police. If your child is in immediate danger, call the emergency number first.
disclaimer: SafeStart is not an emergency service and cannot take reports. This page points you to the organizations that can. Every link and phone number here was checked against the organization's own website on the date shown.
